title: HTTP/HTTPS
subtitle: Stateless request-response semantics, method idempotency, status code precision, caching headers, and TLS edge termination.
keyTakeaways: HTTP methods carry explicit idempotency contracts: GET, PUT, and DELETE must be safely repeatable, whereas POST is non-idempotent and can mutate state on retries.
Status code precision matters in production: 502 indicates an upstream server crashed or returned invalid data, whereas 504 means the upstream gateway timed out waiting for a response.
Terminating TLS at edge load balancers or CDNs offloads cryptographic handshake compute from application containers while preserving end-to-end security via private VPC networking.

sections.heading: HTTP Semantics, Idempotency, and Status Code Precision
sections.body: HTTP is a stateless client-server protocol where every request carries its own context. In distributed systems, understanding method idempotency is essential for safe retry policies: an idempotent operation produces the same server state regardless of whether it executes once or ten times. If a network blip causes a client to timeout on a POST request, naively retrying it risks charging a credit card twice unless guarded by an idempotency key.
bullets: Idempotency Guarantees: GET, HEAD, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent by specification; POST and PATCH are non-idempotent.

Authentication vs Authorization: HTTP 401 Unauthorized means the client provided no credentials or invalid credentials; HTTP 403 Forbidden means the client is authenticated but lacks required permissions.

Gateway Errors: HTTP 502 Bad Gateway means the reverse proxy received an invalid response or connection reset from the upstream service; HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout means the upstream service failed to respond before the proxy's timeout expired.

sections.heading: HTTPS and TLS Edge Termination
sections.body: HTTPS wraps plaintext HTTP in Transport Layer Security (TLS), providing confidentiality, data integrity, and server authentication. In high-traffic architectures, terminating TLS at the edge load balancer or CDN prevents application pods from burning CPU cycles on cryptographic handshakes, while injecting headers like `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` so backend services know the real client IP and protocol.
bullets: Edge Termination: Cryptographic handshakes end at the edge proxy (Cloudflare, AWS ALB, NGINX); traffic travels unencrypted over private isolated VPC subnets.
Full End-to-End Encryption: Strict compliance regimes (PCI-DSS, HIPAA) mandate re-encrypting traffic between the load balancer and internal pods, typically via lightweight mutual TLS (mTLS).
HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS): Instructs browsers via response headers to automatically convert all insecure HTTP requests to HTTPS before hitting the wire.

tradeOffs.pros: Drastically reduces CPU overhead on application fleets; centralizes certificate renewals and cipher suite management.
tradeOffs.cons: Traffic inside the internal VPC runs in plaintext unless governed by VPC network access control lists.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Standard web and mobile API backends running inside isolated cloud VPCs.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees cryptographic privacy across every hop; authenticates service identity between microservices.
tradeOffs.cons: Adds handshake latency and CPU overhead on pod-to-pod communication; requires automated certificate rotation infrastructure (SPIFFE/Vault).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Banking cores, medical record platforms, multi-tenant container platforms, and PCI-compliant systems.

interviewTip: When explaining an API failure scenario in an interview, distinguish clearly between a 502 and a 504. Stating that a 504 means the upstream microservice timed out while a 502 indicates it crashed or reset the TCP socket immediately shows real debugging experience.
